Question: What is the Uncanny Valley?
Answer: For those of you who are unaware the Uncanny Valley is a hypothesis which states as a character gets closer to looking truly human it begins to get creepy and scares human observers Have you ever noticed a human in a movie or video game that doesn’t look quite right? The uncanny valley is a common unsettling feeling people experience when androids (humanoid robots) and audio/visual simulations closely resemble humans in many respects but are not quite convincingly realistic. Essentially we stop responding positively to the similarities we see between ourselves and these robot likenesses because we also see dissimilar features that look like mistakes and imperfections. It can be observed across the field of robotics computer animation movies but the modern term was coined by Japanese robotics professor Masahiro Mori in 1970. This weird robot triggered humans who entered the Uncanny Valley To put it in other terms the Uncanny Valley is the relationship any degree of an object’s resemblance to a human being and the emotional response such an object invokes in a human being. Uncanny Valley The problem is that our human brains have a hard time squaring the idea of humanoid objects which imperfectly resemble actual human beings which somehow can perfectly capture human emotions. Robot and Inventor which provoked the Uncanny Valley in many people Our brains are triggered by the Uncanny Valley which provoke an uncanny or strangely familiar feeling of eeriness and revulsion in observers. The graphic has two axis: The uncanny valley has been observed in a variety of contexts, from highly realistic robots to video game characters. Some of the best-known examples of the uncanny valley can be seen on film. These include: Final Fantasy The 2001 movie Final Fantasy: The Spirits Withinshowcased some of the most realistic CGI animation ever used at that time. Despite efforts to make the animated characters appear super-realistic, the movie was a flop. The film’s commercial failure at the box office is often attributed to the Uncanny Valley. Simply put, people didn’t want to watch the movie because they found the animation disturbing. Shrek The early test screenings of the film Shrek elicited unexpected feelings of anxiety in children in response to the character Princess Fiona. She was simply too lifelike, causing kids to feel unnerved and even frightened, many crying whenever she appeared onscreen. Based on the responses and feedback, the filmmakers edited her appearance prior to the film's theatrical release to give her a more cartoon-like appearance in order to prevent the uncanny valley effect. Cats The 2019 film-adaptation of Cats featured humanoid felines that many people found unsettling. While some reportedly found the effect humorous, others reported feeling downright revolted. On social media, many viewers described the film as weird, creepy, and even nightmare-inducing. The fact that the film relies so heavily on movement may have also played a role in the audience’s reaction. Mori has proposed that the addition of motion can amplify the uncanny valley effect, and in this case, the film includes both human-like movements as well as cat-like motions that serve to further confuse the viewer. Polar Express The Polar Express garnered a lot of hype both for the advanced special effects and the retelling of the classic children's story that has become a staple in many households. In the development of the film, Zemekis wanted the effects to be as human-like as possible: “The problem with traditional animation for a project like this is that it falls short in depicting authentic human characters. With exaggerated images, fantasies like Snow White and the Seven Dwarves, or cartoons, it’s great. But I was looking for something more realistically alive.” Little did Zemekis know that he was so successful they would have the opposite effect on viewers. The film utilized a form of CGI called the “Performance Capture.” This technology existed back in 2004 but was never used to such an extent as Zemekis planned. The Polar Express was the very first feature film to be completely shot through Performance Capture. This technique allowed an actor to become a human blueprint as a multitude of computerized cameras capture every 360 degree movement down to a twitch of the finger. These movements were then used for mapping the animated character. Planet of Apes My mom’s personal fear comes from the uncanny valley when she viewed the new planet of the apes movie. It freaks her out and she cannot watch them because they’re too human like. It’s not a surprise at all these movies were monumental bombs (except for Shek and Planet of the Apes). Many people attribute this to the fact that these movies breached the Unhappy Valley. The uncanny valley is this pattern where, as something becomes more human, we have more positive feelings about it up to a point. When it is kind of human but not quite human, that makes us really uncomfortable. It's that strange familiarity, or familiar strangeness (I like to use this phrase when describing it). So in conclusion I think that we have already breached the point of reaching the unhappy valley in both games and movies and robotics. I hope that clears up any confusion! The Trojans during this time period were also allies of the mighty Hittite Empire (Troy was called Wilusa by the Hittites). There is some evidence that the treaty between the two nations promised troop support to each other. It is believed the Hittites offered troops who fought with the Trojans against the Greeks (and there is some evidence that Trojans joined the Hittites against Egypt at the Battle of Kadesh). Troy was rich and prosperous through its many years of trade and its control over the waterways. They could also reimburse the Hittite Empire. Trojans on their mighty walls Troy was a city that had existed for thousand of years and the Troy of the Trojan War is designated Troy VI. Troy VI It represents a time when the city flourished, the population grew, industry thrived, and grandiose houses were built. It was a settlement of about 1,500 -2,000 inhabitants and the new settlers chose the area because if was the setting of the Trojan War. Question: Why were the Moai statues built?
Answer: The Moai statues on Rapa Nui (Easter Island) served a number of purposes but their location and size indicated the presence of fresh water The inhabitants of Rapa Nui built the Moai as a way to honor and represent their ancestors. But much of what we thought we knew about the Moai and the people who built them has changed. Rapa Nui or Easter Island was discovered by Dutch explorers In 1722. The inhabitants of Rapa Nui first arrived on the island’s shores between 1150 and 1280 A.D. They lived in isolation until 1722. Scientists and archaeologists have long wondered how the people of Rapa Nui chose the locations where their Moai statues were built. Scientists have also long wondered how the people of Rapa Nui could have survived since Easter island gets little to no rainfall and and has no above ground streams or rivers flowing across it. And yet the inhabitants of Easter Island thrived for hundred of years and the community grew to its largest consisting of 10,000 people at its zenith. The location of fresh water had been a mystery for hundreds of years until recently. Researchers began to look at the locations of the ahu (the flat mounds) that the Moai were built upon for any possible water sources. Scientists with satellite technology discovered drinkable but brackish freshwater flowed out of the ground near the coast at low tide. After close inspection, they found that the many Moai were located and guarding the places near the coast where freshwater was available. The Moai marked the location of the few but vital freshwater sources. “Here, we use spatially-explicit point-process modeling to explore the potential relations between ahu construction locations and subsistence resources, namely, rock mulch agricultural gardens, marine resources, and freshwater sources—the three most critical resources on Rapa Nui. Through these analyses, we demonstrate the central importance of coastal freshwater seeps for precontact populations.” “Our results suggest that ahu locations are most parsimoniously explained by distance from freshwater sources, in particular coastal seeps, with important implications for community formation and inter-community competition in precontact times.” Source: Rapa Nui (Easter Island) monument (ahu) locations explained by freshwater sources The team found that rainwater at Easter Island sinks directly through porous bedrock into an underground aquifer (a body of porous rock or sediment where water is concentrated). Wherever the scientific team found water seeping out of the coast, they found platforms for statues. And even in areas in the interior where there were platforms but didn't seem to be any water, they found the remains of ancient wells that tapped the islands underground aquifers. Coastal Seep behind Ahu Tongariki This then surfaces along the coastline as something known as coastal seeps, pockets of freshwater that trickle into the ocean. The scientific team found that in addition to harvesting freshwater from pockets of coastal seep, Rapa Nui’s inhabitants built underwater dams in the ocean to keep fresh and seawater separated and constructed wells that redirected water from the aquifer before reaching the sea. The team also found that the size of the statues seemed to correspond to the amount of the water that was available. In areas completely devoid of freshwater resources, there were no moai or ahu. “Every time we saw massive amounts of fresh water, we saw giant statues,” co-author Carl Lipo from Binghamton University tells Davis. “It was ridiculously predictable.” Source: Easter Island statues marked fresh water supplies This recent study also contradicted the long-held belief that inhabitants of Rapa Nui suffered an ecological collapse as the different warring tribes scrambled for resources. Traditionally, scientists incorrectly believed that competition for resources led to warfare between the various tribes that lived on the island and the competition to build larger statues lead to the society’s eventual collapse. Instead, this new study discovered that the inhabitants and various tribes were cooperative with each other both in the construction of the Moai and in sharing resources most importantly water.
